figures.caption: Figure 4: SLAKE-En test::12035 (left, xmlab160) and its PMC-OA-beta nearest neighbour (right, PMC2531090 Fig. 1) under SigLIP-SO400M, cosine distance 0.0152. The same benchmark example fires the image-NN detector, the Qwen2.5-VL loss-attack flag, and the Qwen2.5-VL Min-K%++ shortlist: an intersection-of-three signal. The two images are the same frontal chest-radiograph view of different patients

Table 1: End-to-end detector calibration. The image-NN false-positive rate is bracketed: 0% on out-of-domain images and ∼0.9% on clean in-domain images (matching the nominal α under SO400M). The final row reports how often canonical-order exchangeability returns raw p < 0.01 on the held-out audit grid (an audit-positive rate, not a false-positive rate).

Table 3: Systematic tail-enrichment scan on the held-out audit, with raw exchangeability p-values refined at 10 000 permutations under deterministic per-cell seeds and Bonferroni-adjusted pBonf = min(1,m · p) over the full m = 27 audit grid (6 OmniMedVQA cells + 21 held-out cells, the latter spanning 3 benchmarks × 7 models; the seven comprise five medical/general VLMs and two external non-medical baselines, BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP). The 12 medical held-out cells are shown here; the baseline cells appear in Table 5 and Section 4.7. The cohort-relative ∆ columns are computed against the four-model medical cohort and are held fixed across the paper. EXCH marks cells with raw exchangeability p < 0.01; TAIL marks cells with Pr[∆ > 100] > 5%. † PathVQA×LLaVA-OneVision passes EXCH on raw p but is reclassified as a release-order artefact by the ordering ablation (Section 4.7) and falls below Bonferroni significance at α = 0.05 on the 27-cell grid (pBonf = 5.4%). SLAKE-En×Qwen2.5-VL (pBonf = 1.35%) is the only held-out cell that survives

Figure 1: Canonical-order exchangeability p-values across the 3× 4 (benchmark, model) grid; darker shading denotes a smaller p-value. Cells marked with an asterisk (and a bold red outline) have p < 0.01. Two cells fire the exchangeability detector at this threshold (Qwen2.5-VL×SLAKE-En, p = 0.002; LLaVA-OneVision×PathVQA, p = 0.002); only the first of the two survives the ordering ablation in Section 4.7. Table 9: Each claim, its status under control, and where it is established.

Figure 3: Threshold (τ = Qα) sensitivity of the image-NN detector. (a) Fraction of images flagged versus the null-quantile level α for SLAKE-En (solid) and the PathVQA control (dashed), on both SigLIP backbones; the dotted line marks the maintext α = 0.01. The SLAKE-En signal is monotone and stays one to two orders of magnitude above the control across the entire sweep. (b) Triple-hit images (image, question, and answer all agreeing) persist across the threshold range and are already nonzero at α = 0.01. Re-plotted from committed sweep data by scripts/tau_sensitivity.py.

Table 8: Manual adjudication of all 20 distinct SLAKE-En images flagged by the image nearest-neighbour detector under either SigLIP backbone, ordered by strictest (smallest) cosine distance. Distances are to the nearest PMC-OA-beta figure. Every flagged pair is the same imaging modality and projection; the verdict records whether visual inspection of the rendered panel (outputs/adjudication/) supports an exact duplicate. Exact pixel-duplication is supported in at most one case; the remaining pairs are same-view images of different patients.
Table 2: OmniMedVQA auxiliary text-side extension on the public 4,999-example mirror. Exchangeability is reported at 10 000-permutation resolution (floor 10−4) using
Figure 2: Per-benchmark fraction of test images flagged by the image-NN detector against PMC-OA-beta, under two SigLIP backbones. The dashed line marks the nominal α = 0.01 false-positive rate.

Figure 6: Per-content-type Pr[∆ > 100] on SLAKE-En for the two high-Min-K models. Bar pairs match within 0.5 percentage points across all 10 content types, including the small Plane bucket (n=58, 43.1% vs 43.1%).

Table 5: External-baseline falsification. With BLIP-2 added to the cohort, the SLAKE-En tail-enrichment flag fires for the external baseline itself (top block), and the crossmodel top-25 Jaccard between BLIP-2 and the originally-flagged models is 1.000 on SLAKE-En, 0.515 on PathVQA, and 0.724 on VQA-RAD. Because BLIP-2 cannot share medical-VQA training-data exposure, the shared-exposure interpretation of Detectors 3 and 4 on this cohort is rejected.

Figure 7: Synthetic audit under the calibration model of Equation (1) with no contamination anywhere. (a) Detector 3 tail-enrichment rate Pr[∆ > 100] per model: the two low-gain calibration outliers (grey) register zero, while every above-median-gain model fires, including the clean external baseline (red) at parity with the two “suspect” high-gain models (blue). (b) False-positive flag probability of a single clean high-gain probe as a function of the number of low-gain outliers in the cohort: the probe is never flagged until the cohort median collapses onto the outliers (at two outliers), after which it is flagged in every draw. Both panels are produced by scripts/confound_simulation.py under a fixed seed.

Table 6: SLAKE-En subpopulation flag rate (Pr[∆ > 100]). CheXagent-8b and LLaVAOneVision-7B exhibit near-identical flag rates in every stratum (including the small Plane bucket, n=58) while InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL show no signal anywhere. |gap| is the absolute difference between the two high-Min-K models, in percentage

Figure 5: Pairwise Jaccard similarity of the top-25 most anomalously-easy example sets across the four audited models, per benchmark. CheXagent-8b and LLaVA-OneVision-7B agree on which examples are anomalous on every benchmark; no other pair does. The signal persists on VQA-RAD even though VQA-RAD looks clean under every per-cell detector.

Table 4: Pairwise Jaccard similarity of top-25 most anomalously easy example sets across audited models. E[∩] = K2/n is the expected intersection under iid sampling. CheXagent-8b and LLaVA-OneVision-7B agree at 10×–118× chance on every benchmark, including the otherwise-clean VQA-RAD.
